definition.text: An incentive is anything that persuades a person or organisation to change their behaviour toward a desired outcome.

facts.text: Disincentives work the other way, discouraging certain actions.
Governments, businesses and other organisations commonly use incentives to encourage particular behaviour.
Incentives are often split into intrinsic ones, driven by personal interest or enjoyment, and extrinsic ones, such as pay, recognition or the threat of punishment.
One scheme sorts incentives into financial (material rewards), moral (doing what is seen as right) and coercive (threat of force).
A misaligned incentive arises when parties' goals conflict, which happens in firms and also in environmental policy.
Incentives can produce unintended outcomes.
A 2026 meta-analysis of 2,193 estimates from 88 experiments found that financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

title: Motivation crowding out

definition.text: Motivation crowding out is the effect where offering outside rewards, such as money, weakens people's own inner motivation to do something.

facts.text: Richard Titmuss's 1970 book The Gift Relationship argued that money incentives disrupted social norms around voluntary giving; Bruno Frey coined the term crowding out in 1997.
Paying volunteers can make people see their altruistic acts as done for reward, so their wish to volunteer falls.
Removing temporary incentives can push effort below where it started.
Evidence that crowding out affects blood donation has been mixed, though many other studies support the basic effect.

contested_note: Evidence for crowding out is mixed in some settings, such as blood donation, though widely supported overall.

definition.text: Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction a person gets from consuming one more unit of a good or service.

facts.text: In economics, marginal means a small change from some starting level, such as the benefit of the next piece of chocolate.
Marginal utility can be positive, negative or zero; negative means each extra unit does more harm than good.
Marginal analysis compares the extra benefits of an activity with its extra costs.
Because utility is hard to measure directly, economists use revealed preferences, ranking options by watching what people choose.
Economists developed the idea of marginal utility while trying to explain how prices are set.
Daniel Bernoulli published the first clear statement of the theory in 1738.
Critics note that people may not optimise as the theory assumes, and that utility varies between people and over time.

title: Diminishing marginal utility
article: Marginal utility#Law of diminishing marginal utility

definition.text: The law of diminishing marginal utility says that each extra unit of something consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before.

facts.text: Three pieces of candy beat two, but the twentieth adds little beyond the nineteenth and may even make things worse.
The principle is reflected in the concave shape of most utility functions.
It helps explain things such as time preference and the value of goods.
Bernoulli and Cramer concluded that money becomes less desirable as more of it accumulates.
Risk aversion is mainly attributed to decreasing marginal utility.

definition.text: The paradox of value, or diamond–water paradox, is the puzzle that water is far more useful for survival than diamonds, yet diamonds fetch a much higher price.

facts.text: Adam Smith is the classic presenter of the paradox, though it appeared as early as Plato.
Smith contrasted value in use with value in exchange: nothing is more useful than water, yet it buys scarcely anything.
Marginalism resolves it: price depends on marginal utility and marginal cost, and the marginal cost of water is lower than that of diamonds.

definition.text: The Marginal Revolution was the spread of marginal utility theory in the 1870s through the work of Jevons in England, Menger in Austria and Walras in Switzerland.

facts.text: Jevons argued that value depends entirely on utility, publishing The Theory of Political Economy in 1871.
Carl Menger presented the theory in his Principles of Economics in 1871, and Walras in 1874.
A second generation, including Alfred Marshall, Böhm-Bawerk, Wieser and Pareto, carried the ideas into the mainstream.
Over the 20th century a large literature grew on the conflict between marginalism and the labour theory of value.
